text: A real deployment doesn't start the moment you open a cloud console. It starts earlier, with a conversation that answers what this workload is actually for, who's going to use it, and what happens if it goes down. Skipping that conversation doesn't save time — it just moves the decisions you're dodging now to a worse moment later, usually after something breaks.

Every real deployment brief answers five questions: expected traffic and load, including when it spikes; compliance requirements tied to the kind of data involved; real budget constraints, not an aspirational number; availability needs, like whether it can go down overnight; and who the users actually are, internal staff or the open internet. None of that requires a console — it requires asking the person who owns the workload.

A real brief can be as short as five lines: the workload, expected users and peak times, the compliance framework if any applies, a monthly budget ceiling, and an availability target such as ninety-nine point five percent during business hours. That's enough to start sizing infrastructure and choosing a provider. Guessing at any one of those lines isn't.

Skip this step and it costs you in one of two directions. Undersized infrastructure, chosen by guessing, buckles the first time real traffic hits it — an outage, not a minor inconvenience. Oversized infrastructure, chosen to be safe, quietly wastes budget every month. Worst of all is a compliance requirement discovered after deployment, which usually means rebuilding encryption, logging, and network isolation into a system that's already live.

That short brief is what the rest of this chapter runs on. Lesson two uses it to choose honestly between cloud providers. Lesson three uses the load numbers to size compute and storage realistically instead of guessing. Lesson four uses all of it to sketch the architecture before anything gets built. Skip the brief, and every decision after it is a guess wearing an engineer's clothes.

You now know the five questions a real deployment answers before any infrastructure gets chosen, and why skipping them turns into rework later. Next: taking that same brief and using it to decide honestly between Azure, AWS, or both for the workload sitting in front of you.
